hook.text: Risk is when you know the odds. Uncertainty is when you don't. Insurance handles risk well. Uncertainty can destroy it.

buildup.text: Frank Knight defined the difference in 1921. A coin flip is risk—50/50.

discovery.text: Insurers thrive on risk because they can calculate premiums.

twist.text: Climate change is shifting risks into uncertainties. Historical data no longer predicts future hurricanes.

climax.text: The boundary between risk and uncertainty defines what's insurable. When that line moves, so does the insurance market.

punchline.text: Known odds: risk. Unknown odds: uncertainty.

quiz.question: What's the key difference between risk and uncertainty?
options: Risk has calculable odds; uncertainty doesn't

hook.text: Flip a coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads. Flip it 10,000 times and you'll get almost exactly 50%.

buildup.text: Insurance works the same way. One person's fate is unpredictable.

discovery.text: An insurer can't predict if you will die this year.

twist.text: The law breaks down with correlated risks.

climax.text: The law of large numbers is insurance's mathematical engine. Pool enough risk and randomness becomes predictable.

punchline.text: One person: unpredictable. One million: almost certain.

quiz.question: Why does the law of large numbers matter for insurance?
options: It makes aggregate risk predictable across large pools

hook.text: You can't insure your neighbor's house. You need 'insurable interest'—a financial stake in what you're insuring.

buildup.text: The rule dates to the 1774 Life Assurance Act.

discovery.text: You have insurable interest in your own life, your spouse's, your business partner's, and your property.

twist.text: Corporations insured janitors without their knowledge—'dead peasant' policies.

climax.text: Insurable interest separates insurance from gambling.

punchline.text: No financial stake, no policy.

quiz.question: What is insurable interest?
options: A financial stake in the insured item or person

hook.text: 10,000 people each pay $1,000 a year. That $10 million pool pays the 50 people who have claims.

buildup.text: Risk pooling is insurance's core mechanism. Many pay in, few claim out.

discovery.text: Pools work best when risks are independent. Car accidents in Texas don't affect car accidents in Maine.

twist.text: Pools fail when risks are correlated. A hurricane hits all Florida policyholders at once.

climax.text: A good risk pool has diverse, independent risks. A bad one has concentrated, correlated ones.

punchline.text: 10,000 pay in, 50 claim.

quiz.question: When do risk pools fail?
options: When risks are correlated and everyone claims at once

hook.text: Insurers separate risk into three parts: a peril causes loss, a hazard increases the chance of a peril.

buildup.text: Fire is a peril. Storing gasoline in your garage is a hazard. Your burned-down house is the loss.

discovery.text: Hazards can be physical (old wiring), moral (intention to commit fraud).

twist.text: Morale hazard is the sneakiest. People with insurance take more risks because they're protected.

climax.text: Understanding hazard, peril, and loss lets insurers price risk precisely.

punchline.text: Peril, hazard, loss. Three words that define how insurers see every risk.

quiz.question: What is a hazard in insurance terms?
options: The financial damage from an event
A condition that increases the likelihood of a peril

hook.text: Actuaries predict the financial cost of future events.

buildup.text: Using statistics, probability, and financial theory.

discovery.text: The actuarial profession is one of the highest-paid.

twist.text: Becoming an actuary requires passing 7-10 brutally difficult exams over 5-7 years.

climax.text: Actuaries are the invisible backbone of insurance.

punchline.text: Math determines your premium.

quiz.question: What is an actuary's primary role?
options: Predicting the financial cost of future risks

hook.text: In 1693, astronomer Edmond Halley built the first mortality table using birth and death records from Breslau, Germany.

buildup.text: Halley tracked how many people died at each age.

discovery.text: His table proved that younger people should pay less for annuities.

twist.text: Halley is better known for predicting his comet.

climax.text: Halley's table turned death from a mystery into a statistic. That single innovation made modern life insurance possible.

punchline.text: An astronomer mapped death by age.

quiz.question: Who created the first mortality table?

hook.text: A loss ratio of 60% means 60 cents of every premium dollar goes to claims.

buildup.text: Insurers track loss ratios obsessively.

discovery.text: The combined ratio adds expenses to losses. Below 100% means underwriting profit.

twist.text: Many insurers operate above 100% on purpose. They lose money on underwriting but profit from investing the premiums.

climax.text: The combined ratio is insurance's scoreboard.

punchline.text: Below 100%: profit. Above 100%: losing money.

quiz.question: What does a combined ratio above 100% indicate?
options: The insurer is losing money on underwriting

topics.title: Reserving: Money Set Aside for Claims

hook.text: Insurers must set aside reserves for claims that haven't been paid yet. Getting reserves wrong can bankrupt the company.

buildup.text: When a claim is reported, the insurer estimates its cost and reserves that amount.

discovery.text: Actuaries use IBNR—'incurred but not reported'.

twist.text: Asbestos bankrupted insurers because reserves were set too low.

climax.text: Reserving is the most important and most uncertain job in insurance. Too low means insolvency.

punchline.text: Too low: bankruptcy. Too high: waste.

quiz.question: What does IBNR stand for?

hook.text: Trust one person's claim history or the population's data? Credibility theory weighs both to set the right premium.

buildup.text: A driver with zero claims in 10 years looks safe. But statistically, anyone can have an accident.

discovery.text: Credibility theory assigns a weight: the more data points you have.

twist.text: New drivers get charged group rates because there's no personal data yet. After five claim-free years.

climax.text: Credibility theory is how insurers personalize premiums.

punchline.text: 0 claims in 10 years? Your data earns trust.

quiz.question: What does credibility theory determine?
options: How to weight individual data vs. group data for pricing
If a policy should be canceled

hook.text: Bayes' theorem updates probability when new evidence arrives.

buildup.text: Thomas Bayes, an 18th-century minister, developed a formula for updating beliefs.

discovery.text: If 1% of policyholders are high-risk, a claim makes the probability jump. Two claims make it near-certain.

twist.text: Bayesian methods now power fraud detection. Each new data point updates the probability of fraud in real time.

climax.text: Bayes' theorem turns data into evolving knowledge. In insurance, every claim updates every prediction.

punchline.text: New data, new odds. Bayes' theorem lets insurance learn from every claim.

quiz.question: How do insurers use Bayes' theorem?
options: To update risk probabilities as new data arrives

hook.text: How many car accidents will happen in a city next year? The Poisson distribution models rare events over set intervals.

buildup.text: Siméon-Denis Poisson published his theory in 1837.

discovery.text: Auto insurers use Poisson to predict claim frequency.

twist.text: The distribution assumes events are independent.

climax.text: Poisson turns rare, random events into predictable patterns.

punchline.text: Rare events form patterns.

quiz.question: What does the Poisson distribution model?
options: The probability of rare events occurring in a fixed period

hook.text: Normal distributions say extreme events are nearly impossible.

buildup.text: A 'fat tail' distribution has higher probability at the extremes.

discovery.text: Long-Term Capital Management used normal distributions in 1998.

twist.text: Insurers who underestimate tail risk go bankrupt.

climax.text: Fat tails warn that the worst-case scenario is more likely than you think.

punchline.text: 1-in-a-billion? It happens. Fat tails punish insurers who trust the bell curve.

quiz.question: What is a fat tail distribution?
options: A distribution where extreme events are more likely than expected

hook.text: Monte Carlo simulations run thousands of random scenarios to estimate risk.

buildup.text: Instead of one prediction, Monte Carlo generates 10,000 possible outcomes.

discovery.text: Insurers use Monte Carlo to test portfolios.

twist.text: The method was developed for nuclear weapons by Stanislaw Ulam in 1946.

climax.text: Monte Carlo doesn't predict the future. It maps the landscape of possibilities, showing insurers where the dangers live.

punchline.text: 10,000 random scenarios.

quiz.question: What do Monte Carlo simulations do for insurers?
options: Run thousands of random scenarios to estimate risk ranges

hook.text: If one house burns, that's one claim. If a wildfire burns 10,000 houses, that's 10,000 simultaneous claims.

buildup.text: Insurance works by spreading independent risks.

discovery.text: Accumulation risk is the total exposure in one area.

twist.text: 9/11 exposed hidden correlations.

climax.text: Correlation is the enemy of insurance diversification. Events that hit everything at once are what bankrupt companies.

punchline.text: One fire: manageable. Ten thousand fires: catastrophe.

quiz.question: Why is correlation dangerous for insurers?
options: Correlated events cause massive simultaneous claims

hook.text: People fear shark attacks but not car crashes. Sharks kill 5 Americans a year. Cars kill 40,000.

buildup.text: Daniel Kahneman discovered that humans overweight vivid, dramatic risks and underweight common, boring ones.

discovery.text: Insurers exploit this. Flood insurance is underpriced because people underestimate flood risk.

twist.text: After 9/11, Americans drove instead of flying. Car accident deaths rose by 1,600 in the next year.

climax.text: Human risk perception is systematically wrong. Insurance pricing corrects for what our intuition gets backward.

punchline.text: Sharks: 5 deaths. Cars: 40,000. We fear the wrong risks every time.

quiz.question: Why do people misjudge risk?
options: They overweight dramatic risks and underweight common ones

hook.text: When you're insured, you take more risks. People with theft insurance lock their doors less.

buildup.text: Moral hazard means the insured person changes behavior because they're protected.

discovery.text: Deductibles combat moral hazard by making you share the cost.

twist.text: The 2008 financial crisis was moral hazard in action.

climax.text: Moral hazard is insurance's central paradox: protection encourages recklessness.

punchline.text: Insured people take more risks. Deductibles exist to keep you careful.

quiz.question: How do insurers reduce moral hazard?
options: By requiring deductibles so policyholders share costs

hook.text: Sick people buy more health insurance. Healthy people buy less.

buildup.text: When only high-risk people buy in, the pool becomes expensive. Higher prices push more healthy people out.

discovery.text: George Akerlof described this as the 'market for lemons'—when buyers know more than sellers, the market collapses.

twist.text: Genetic testing intensifies adverse selection. People who know they carry disease genes buy more coverage.

climax.text: Adverse selection is why mandates exist.

punchline.text: Sick buy in, healthy opt out.

quiz.question: What causes adverse selection?
options: High-risk individuals are more likely to purchase coverage

hook.text: Losing $100 feels twice as painful as gaining $100 feels good. This asymmetry—loss aversion—is why people buy insurance.

buildup.text: Kahneman and Tversky proved that humans hate losses more than they love gains.

discovery.text: Insurance is priced above fair value—the expected loss.

twist.text: Extended warranties exploit loss aversion aggressively.

climax.text: Loss aversion is the emotional engine of insurance.

punchline.text: Losses hurt 2x more than gains.

quiz.question: What is loss aversion?
options: Feeling losses more intensely than equivalent gains

hook.text: After 10 years without a flood, people stop buying flood insurance.

buildup.text: The gambler's fallacy says past random events influence future ones. After five red spins, people bet black.

discovery.text: Flood insurance purchases spike after floods and drop during dry years. Risk doesn't change—only perception does.

twist.text: The same fallacy applies to earthquakes. After a big one, people buy insurance. Five calm years later, they cancel.

climax.text: The gambler's fallacy causes coverage gaps exactly when disasters strike.

punchline.text: No flood in 10 years? Still a flood risk.

quiz.question: What is the gambler's fallacy in insurance?
options: Believing past safety reduces future risk

hook.text: Catastrophe models simulate 10,000 years of hurricanes, earthquakes, and floods on a computer.

buildup.text: Cat models combine physics, engineering, and financial data.

discovery.text: Three companies dominate: RMS, AIR, and CoreLogic.

twist.text: Models disagree wildly. For the same hurricane, one model might predict $50 billion in losses and another $80 billion.

climax.text: Cat models replaced intuition with simulation.

punchline.text: 10,000 virtual years of disasters.

quiz.question: What do catastrophe models simulate?
options: Thousands of years of natural disasters to predict losses

hook.text: After Hurricane Andrew bankrupted 11 insurers in 1992.

buildup.text: Before Andrew, insurers used historical averages. A bad year was just bad luck.

discovery.text: Clark's model simulated hurricane paths and building vulnerabilities.

twist.text: Her company, AIR Worldwide, was initially ignored. Insurers didn't trust computers over experience.

climax.text: Karen Clark's model became the standard. Today, no property insurer operates without catastrophe modeling.

punchline.text: 11 bankruptcies, one model.

quiz.question: What triggered the creation of catastrophe modeling?

hook.text: A catastrophe bond lets investors bet against disasters. If no hurricane hits, they earn 10%+ returns.

buildup.text: Insurers issue cat bonds to transfer extreme risk to Wall Street.

discovery.text: The cat bond market reached $45 billion in 2023.

twist.text: Cat bonds pay investors when nothing bad happens.

climax.text: Cat bonds connected insurance to capital markets.

punchline.text: $45 billion market. Wall Street now bets on whether hurricanes will hit.

quiz.question: What happens to catastrophe bond investors when a disaster strikes?

hook.text: Climate models predict decades-long trends. Insurance models predict next year's losses.

buildup.text: Climate science says hurricanes will intensify over 50 years.

discovery.text: Insurers are integrating climate projections into cat models.

twist.text: Some insurers are racing ahead of climate science, raising premiums today for tomorrow's risk.

climax.text: The clash between climate and insurance models defines the industry's future.

punchline.text: Climate: 50-year trends. Insurance: next year's losses.

quiz.question: Why is integrating climate models into insurance pricing difficult?

hook.text: How do you model a risk that's never happened? Cyber attacks, AI liability.

buildup.text: Traditional actuarial science needs decades of data. Emerging risks offer years at most.

discovery.text: Scenario-based modeling fills the gap.

twist.text: The insurance industry was slow to model cyber risk.

climax.text: Emerging risks are the frontier of insurance science.

punchline.text: No data, no history. Emerging risks force insurers to model the unprecedented.

quiz.question: How do insurers model risks with no historical data?
options: Scenario-based modeling with expert-estimated worst cases

hook.text: Nassim Taleb coined 'Black Swan' for events that are rare, unpredictable, and devastating.

buildup.text: Models can't predict Black Swans because they lie outside historical experience.

discovery.text: Taleb argues that instead of predicting Black Swans, you should build systems that survive them.

twist.text: After every Black Swan, people claim it was obvious in hindsight.

climax.text: Black Swans define the limits of insurance. Some events can't be modeled, priced, or predicted.

punchline.text: Rare, unpredictable, devastating. Black Swans break every insurance model.

quiz.question: What is a Black Swan event?
options: A rare, unpredictable event with massive impact

hook.text: Models are only as good as their assumptions. When those assumptions are wrong, the model can be dangerously misleading.

buildup.text: Before Hurricane Katrina, models assumed New Orleans levees would hold. They didn't.

discovery.text: Model risk is the risk that your model is wrong.

twist.text: AIG's financial collapse in 2008 was partly model failure. Their risk models said mortgage defaults wouldn't correlate.

climax.text: Models are essential but fallible. The most dangerous belief in insurance is that the model is always right.

punchline.text: Wrong assumptions, wrong predictions.

quiz.question: What is model risk?
options: The risk that a predictive model's assumptions are wrong

hook.text: Some risks can't be insured at any price.

buildup.text: For a risk to be insurable, it must be quantifiable, independent, and affordable.

discovery.text: Climate change is pushing more risks toward uninsurability.

twist.text: When private insurance retreats, governments step in—or people go unprotected.

climax.text: The uninsurability frontier is expanding.

punchline.text: Nuclear war, asteroid impact: uninsurable.

quiz.question: What makes a risk uninsurable?
options: It's not quantifiable, independent, or affordable

hook.text: Regulators force insurers to prove they can survive a 1-in-200-year disaster.

buildup.text: Solvency II in Europe requires insurers to hold enough capital to survive a 99.5% confidence level of losses.

discovery.text: Stress tests simulate extreme scenarios: a pandemic plus an earthquake plus a market crash.

twist.text: Some argue stress tests create false confidence. If the 1-in-200-year event is wrong, the test is meaningless.

climax.text: Stress tests are imperfect but indispensable.

punchline.text: Survive a 1-in-200-year storm—on paper.

quiz.question: What do regulatory stress tests require insurers to demonstrate?
options: Ability to survive extreme disaster scenarios

hook.text: Prediction markets let people bet on future events.

buildup.text: Platforms aggregate thousands of opinions into a single probability.

discovery.text: Some insurers experiment with prediction markets internally.

twist.text: Prediction markets fail when participants lack information or when events are truly unprecedented.

climax.text: Prediction markets offer a new tool for risk assessment.

punchline.text: Bet on the future. Prediction markets sometimes beat expert models.

quiz.question: How do prediction markets work?
options: People bet on future events, creating aggregate probabilities
